interest: ONI details Japan's 4.5-million-yen U.S. propaganda budget; Dr. Rosetta S. Hall turns an aid appeal into pro-Japanese defense.
keywords: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.00P, covering March to September 1940 with related cross-references through April 1941) documents Japanese propaganda operations in the United States and the contentious domestic debate over American policy toward East Asia. Transmitted largely through correspondence between Roger S. Greene of the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression and Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations, the file contains sample issues of the pro-Japanese publication The Japanese-American Review, isolationist rejoinders from retired missionary physician Dr. Rosetta S. Hall, and anti-conscription mobilization bulletins from Frederick J. Libby's National Council for Prevention of War. Complementing these public diplomacy artifacts are an Office of Naval Intelligence report disclosing Japanese government expenditures and organizational disputes surrounding overseas propaganda, consular cross-reference sheets investigating phonograph records as propaganda media, and a Division of Far Eastern Affairs economic memorandum on inflationary pressures and bond absorption in wartime Japan.

subfiles.about: Clippings from The Japanese-American Review of January 27, 1940, featuring articles defending Japan's New Order in East Asia and opposing trade embargoes.
subfiles.from: The Japanese-American Review (Kaname Wakasugi, Hartley B. Whyte, William R. Castle)
subfiles.summary: A collection of clippings from the January 27, 1940 issue of The Japanese-American Review. It includes an address by Consul General Kaname Wakasugi at the City Club of New York comparing Japan's 'New Order in East Asia' to the Monroe Doctrine and the New Deal while pledging to maintain the Open Door. The clippings also feature an extended article by Hartley B. Whyte analyzing the expiration of the 1911 commercial treaty, heavily citing former Undersecretary of State William R. Castle, Walter Lippmann, and Congressional leaders who warned that an embargo against Japan would lead to war, devastate Southern cotton growers, and drive Japan toward the Soviet Union.
subfiles.title: Clippings from The Japanese-American Review (January 27, 1940) on East Asia Policy and Trade Embargoes

subfiles.about: Clippings from The Japanese-American Review of August 10, 1940, emphasizing Soviet machinations to provoke a U.S.-Japan war and oil supply alternatives.
subfiles.from: The Japanese-American Review (H. D. Collier, Boake Carter, editorial staff)
subfiles.summary: Clippings from the August 10, 1940 issue of The Japanese-American Review presenting multiple arguments against U.S. sanctions on Japan. An interview with Standard Oil Company of California president H. D. Collier warns of massive corporate losses and asserts that Japan can readily secure petroleum from the Dutch East Indies, Latin America, or the USSR. Further articles include a syndicated column by Boake Carter branding export licenses as dangerous sanctions, reports on the formation of the second Konoye Cabinet, and feature essays claiming Moscow is using American Communist transmission belts to push the United States into war with Japan to further Soviet domination in Asia.
subfiles.title: Clippings from The Japanese-American Review (August 10, 1940) on Soviet Intrigue and Oil Sanctions
